title: Checking vs. Savings Account: What’s the Difference?
summary: Learn the fundamental differences between checking and savings accounts and choose the right option for your financial needs.

- Checking vs. Savings Account: What’s the Difference?


If you’ve just started managing your own money, you’ve probably heard about the two main types of bank accounts: checking and savings. Since[94% of U.S. adults](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-executive-summary.htm) had a bank account in 2025, according to the Federal Reserve, chances are you already have one of these types of accounts. Still, you might not be sure how they differ or which one you need.


Building your[financial literacy](https://www.intuit.com/financial-literacy/) starts with basics like these. This article explains the differences between checking vs. savings accounts, the fees you might pay, how much to keep in each, and why most people use both.


## Key takeaways


- A checking account is for everyday spending and bills. A savings account holds money you don’t plan to spend soon and pays interest on it.
- Savings usually pays more. In the FDIC’s October 19, 2026 update, national averages were 0.38% for savings and 0.07% for interest checking.
- The federal six-withdrawal limit on savings ended in 2020, but your bank may still set its own limit.
- Both are insured. At FDIC-insured banks, coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. At federally insured credit unions, each member has at least $250,000.
- Most people do best with both. Keep enough in checking to cover what’s due before your next paycheck, and move the rest to savings.


## The difference between checking and savings accounts


At the most basic level, the difference between a checking account vs. a savings account is this: You use a checking account for general everyday spending and a savings account to save funds and earn interest.


You can quickly and easily access funds stored in a checking account to use for everyday expenses on an ongoing basis.


As the name implies, money saved in a savings account builds toward more long-term financial goals. Think things like purchasing a home, funding retirement, or saving for a child’s education. Savings accounts earn interest over time to aid in those efforts. Ideally, you’ll limit withdrawals from your savings account to maximize the interest benefit.


Here is a comparison chart highlighting the main differences between the two account types:


**Checking account** **Savings account**


***Purpose*** Withdraw money for everyday spending and transactions Save money for long-term goals and earn interest


***Access to funds*** Easily accessible; frequent withdrawals Some banks limit withdrawals; not built for daily expenses


***Interest earned*** Generally lower or no interest; national average 0.07% for interest checking Usually higher; national average 0.38% for savings, per the FDIC’s Oct. 19, 2026 update


***Fees*** Basic accounts are often free or waive the monthly fee; interest checking usually charges one unless you keep a minimum balance May charge a monthly fee; some banks waive it if you keep a minimum balance


***Minimum balance requirement*** Low or none for basic accounts; higher for interest checking Often requires a minimum balance for optimal interest


## What is a checking account?


A checking account enables you to make unlimited deposits and withdrawals through various methods. You can transfer funds, make payments, and use automatic teller machines (ATMs) to withdraw or deposit funds whenever you want.


Most people use checking for everyday spending and bills. You can open one individually or with a partner in the form of a joint account. If you’re combining money with a partner, it helps to[talk through your finances together](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/how-to-have-a-conversation-about-finances-with-your-partner/) first.


Checking accounts were originally named such because they allowed you to write paper checks. You can still do that, but checks made up just[4% of noncash payments by number in 2024](https://www.federalreserve.gov/paymentsystems/frps_cy2015_24_topline.htm) , down from 59% in 2000, according to the Federal Reserve. More and more, people are using debit cards linked to their checking accounts or payment apps to transact.


You can open a checking account through financial institutions like banks or credit unions. Look for banks that offer[Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)](https://www.fdic.gov/resources/deposit-insurance/faq) insured accounts or federally insured credit unions covered through the[National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund](https://ncua.gov/support-services/share-insurance-fund) .


These insured accounts cover your deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. At an FDIC-insured bank, joint accounts are insured up to $250,000 per co-owner, so a joint account with two owners can be covered up to $500,000. This means that if the bank or credit union fails, you should be able to retrieve your funds up to the defined limit.


### How to access money in a checking account


Financial institutions provide various ways to use and access your checking account funds for seamless money transfer. This includes debit cards, checkbooks, and mobile and online banking apps. You can also withdraw and deposit cash using an ATM. Many use their banking apps to manage their funds, track expenses, or send money to other people, often via third-party transfer services.


An external bank transfer, often via the[Automated Clearing House (ACH) network](https://www.nacha.org/content/how-ach-payments-work) , a US electronic network that facilitates financial transactions, is another popular option for sending money to another bank account. Many use these types of transfers to pay bills (utilities, rent, mortgage, credit cards, etc.) and receive direct deposits. Bill payments often require you to provide your checking account’s routing and account numbers to the provider, though many banks enable you to make and schedule them through their online or mobile platforms.


Your credit card will be separate, even if it’s with the same bank. You’ll make credit card payments by transferring money from your checking account.


### Checking account fees


Many checking accounts charge fees, though basic accounts often skip the monthly fee or waive it. In[Bankrate’s 2025 checking survey](https://www.bankrate.com/banking/checking/checking-account-survey/) , 47% of non-interest checking accounts charged no monthly fee, and another 48% waived it with direct deposit. Some recur monthly, while others you pay every time you access a certain service.


Here are checking account fees you may see:


- **Maintenance fees:** Charged every month or year
- **Overdraft fees:** Applied when you spend more than your account balance. In the Federal Reserve’s 2025 household survey, 12% of adults with a bank account said they paid an overdraft fee in the prior year.
- **ATM fees:** For using out-of-network ATMs
- **Paper statement fees:** For receiving printed documents or reports
- **Foreign transaction fees:** For exchanging or making transactions involving foreign currencies
- **Wire transfer fees:** For sending or receiving wire transfers
- **Excess transaction fees:** For exceeding the allowed number of transactions per month


Your bank’s fee schedule lists the exact amounts. Ask for it before you open the account.


### Benefits of checking accounts


A checking account has several advantages. Some of the most common include:


- **Withdraw your money anytime, anywhere:** You can access an expansive network of ATMs to withdraw your funds using a debit card.
- **Get paid quickly and without added risks:** You can set up direct deposits with your employer to get your money right away on payday.
- **Bill payment services:** Many checking accounts allow you to automate and manage your recurring payments, such as bills and monthly subscription fees.
- **Keep a record of your transactions:** Through online banking and mobile apps, you can oversee your financial transactions and keep your monthly expenses and balance under control.
- **Protection for your deposits:** Insured accounts protect your money up to the coverage limits if the bank or credit union fails.


## What are savings accounts?


A savings account is where you store money and earn interest. The interest helps your savings grow faster. Rates vary by bank, credit union and account type.


How much interest you earn depends on the account’s annual percentage yield (APY). For example, an account with a 1% APY will earn $10 on a $1,000 balance over a year, if the balance and rate stay the same. Rates vary widely. The[FDIC’s national average for savings was 0.38%](https://www.fdic.gov/national-rates-and-rate-caps) in its October 19, 2026 update, while[Bankrate’s list of high-yield accounts](https://www.bankrate.com/banking/savings/best-high-yield-interests-savings-accounts/) put the top savings rate at 4.35% APY on October 23, 2026. Most savings rates are variable, so they can change after you open the account.


Say you keep $1,000 in savings for a year. At the 0.38% national average, it earns about $3.80. At 4.35%, it earns about $43.50. That gap is why it pays to compare rates before you open an account.


### How to access money in a savings account


Savings accounts are built for holding money, so they’re less convenient to spend from than checking. The usual way to use the money is to transfer it to your checking account, online or in your bank’s app.


You may have heard that savings accounts allow only six withdrawals a month. That was a federal rule until April 2020, when the[Federal Reserve deleted the six-per-month limit](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/bcreg20200424a.htm) from its savings deposit definition. The Fed lets banks drop the limit but doesn’t require them to, so some still cap withdrawals, and banks can charge a fee when you go over. Check your account terms.


You don’t have to withdraw the interest you’ve earned. Leaving it in the account lets it compound, which helps your balance grow faster over time.


This design makes savings accounts a go-to option for storing your money instead of using it regularly. When comparing savings vs. checking accounts, the fact that savings accounts earn interest and often limit transactions stands out as the most glaring difference.


### Savings account fees


Savings accounts are mostly for growing your money, but they can charge fees too. You can often avoid or waive them.


Here are fees you may see and ways you might be able to get around them:


- **Monthly maintenance fees:** These are usually waived by maintaining a minimum balance.
- **Excess withdrawal fees:** These are often avoided by using your checking account to make withdrawals.
- **Paper statement fees:** These are often waived by opting for electronic statements through online banking.
- **Account closure fees:** To avoid these fees, check the minimum time you need to keep the account open before closing it.
- **Inactivity fees:** Make regular deposits or use your savings account to pay recurring monthly bills to keep the account active.


Note that whether these workarounds apply to your savings account will depend on the specific terms and conditions set by your bank or credit union.


### Benefits of savings accounts


There are various benefits to opening a savings account. Here are some of the most common advantages:


- **Earn interest on your account balances:** This is the most basic yet biggest benefit of having a savings account.
- **Easier to save:** Some banks limit withdrawals, and moving money to checking adds a step, so it’s harder to spend on impulse.
- **Fulfills a variety of financial goals:**[Saving money](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/start-saving-money/) is the first step toward many life goals, such as a down payment or retirement.
- **A ladder to higher investments:** You can learn how to better manage your money and build wealth or take the next step into higher-stakes investments.
- **Peace of mind in case of emergencies:** A savings account gives you money to draw on when something goes wrong, like losing your job or a surprise medical bill. In a[September 2026 Intuit Credit Karma survey](https://www.creditkarma.com/about/commentary/most-americans-faced-an-unexpected-expense-this-year-and-many-arent-ready-for-the-next) conducted by The Harris Poll, 37% of Americans said they don’t feel financially prepared to handle a major unexpected expense.


## Where money market accounts fit


A money market account is a type of savings account. It tends to pay more interest than other savings accounts, according to the[Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-money-market-account-en-1007/) . Like other deposit accounts, it’s insured by the FDIC or NCUA. They usually limit how many transactions you can make by check, debit card, or electronic transfer.


In the same FDIC update, the national average for money market accounts was 0.63%, compared with 0.38% for savings. Don’t confuse a money market account with a money market mutual fund. The fund is an investment, and the CFPB notes it isn’t a savings or checking account.


## How much to keep in checking: the one-paycheck buffer


If you keep both accounts, the next question is how to split your money. The one-paycheck buffer gives you a number to aim for:


1. List what’s due before your next paycheck. Rent, bills, autopays, subscriptions and the spending you expect, such as groceries and gas.
2. Add a cushion you choose. This covers a bill that comes in higher than usual, so an autopay doesn’t overdraw the account.
3. Keep that total in checking. On payday, move anything above it to savings. A budget like the[50/30/20 rule](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/boost-your-financial-fitness-with-the-50-30-20-rule/) can help you see what’s left to save.


Say you’re paid $2,000 every two weeks, and $1,400 in rent share, bills and spending lands before the next check. With a $200 cushion, your checking target is $1,600, so $400 can go to savings each payday. The[CFPB suggests](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/an-essential-guide-to-building-an-emergency-fund/) setting up a recurring transfer from checking to savings, so the money moves without you having to remember.


Where you keep the savings depends on your habits:


- If you’re tempted to dip into savings, keep it at a different bank than your checking. A transfer between banks can take a business day or two, which gives you time to rethink a purchase.
- If convenience matters more, keep both at one bank. You can move money between them in the same app, and you can link savings to checking for overdraft protection. The[CFPB notes](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/bank-accounts/know-your-overdraft-options/) you may be charged a transfer fee, but less than the fee for an overdraft.
- If you’re a teen or opening your first account, read up on the basics of[financial literacy for teens and young adults](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/financial-literacy-teens-young-adults/) before you choose a bank.
- If you’re building a safety net, treat savings as your[emergency fund](https://www.intuit.com/blog/social-responsibility/the-emergency-fund-why-you-need-one-and-how-to-get-started/) . The CFPB says the right amount depends on your situation.


If you also earn money from a side business, keep it in its own account. The same logic of separating money by purpose applies, and it protects you from spending money you’ve set aside for taxes or supplies. Cash timing is a common strain. In the[Intuit QuickBooks 2026 Small Business Late Payments Report](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/r/small-business-data/small-business-late-payments-report-2026/) , 49% of small business owners said standard payment processing times create critical or moderate cash-flow gaps. On the Mind the Business podcast, one founder explained why he splits incoming money across several accounts:


> “…I have to protect the business from myself. That’s what that system does. Keeps me from being irresponsible with my money.”
>
>
> Evan Van Auken, founder of Scorch Marker, on[“The Hidden Work of Business”](https://omny.fm/shows/mind-the-business-small-business-success-stories/the-hidden-work-of-business)


## Should you have a checking account or a savings account?


After comparing checking vs. savings accounts, you may decide it makes sense to have both. You can handle everyday spending with ease and still have a place to save toward your goals. It’s typically easy to open both types of accounts at the same financial institution.


If you’re interested in learning more about becoming an expert in your own personal finances, check out our[personal finance courses](https://www.intuit.com/solutions/education/learners/) for individual learners. Build your financial confidence today.


## Common questions about checking and savings accounts


### Can you write checks from a savings account?


Usually not. Many savings accounts don’t come with checks. Money market accounts are the exception: the CFPB notes they may let you write a limited number of checks.


### Is a debit card linked to a checking or savings account?


Usually a checking account. In 2024, non-prepaid debit cards linked to checking accounts made up 82% of debit card payments by number, according to the[Federal Reserve Payments Study](https://www.federalreserve.gov/paymentsystems/frps_cy2015_24_topline.htm) .


### Do savings accounts still limit withdrawals to six a month?


There is no federal six-withdrawal limit anymore. The Federal Reserve removed it in April 2020, but banks may keep their own limits or fees, so check your account terms.
